analysis.one_liner: Makes permanent the lower tax rates on capital gains and stock dividends.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 18 Republican senators, never received a vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 tax cuts that lowered tax rates on capital gains and dividends were scheduled to expire in 2008. This bill would delete that expiration date, making the lower investment tax rates permanent. It was introduced by Senator Mike Crapo with Senate Republican leaders as original cosponsors, but it never received a vote and expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who earn income from capital gains and dividends, which flows overwhelmingly to the wealthiest households. Making the rates permanent would let high-income investors plan around a permanent low rate on investment income rather than a temporary one.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the expiration date that Congress wrote into the 2003 tax law, so the reduced rates on capital gains and dividend income would no longer lapse [S2][S3].

Because capital gains and dividend income are concentrated among the highest-income households, a permanent rate reduction delivers its largest benefits to them; a household whose income comes mostly from wages would see little or no change [S2].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would collect less revenue each year, most of it from high earners who currently owe tax on gains and dividends. That revenue would have to be replaced by other taxes, lower federal spending, or more borrowing.

drawbacks.text: Making the rates permanent converts a temporary tax cut into a permanent reduction in federal revenue, largely from the taxpayers who owe tax on investment income [S2][S3].

Because the benefit flows mainly to households with large investment portfolios, the bill shifts the overall tax burden further toward wage income; supporters would counter that lower investment taxes encourage saving and investment, but permanent revenue loss is the real cost an honest supporter must acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit goes mainly to wealthy households who own most of the country's stocks and assets, while the cost is permanent federal revenue that would otherwise be raised mostly from those same households. There is little in the bill for ordinary wage earners.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended. (Separately, Congress passed a different bill in 2006 that extended the same reduced rates for two more years, so investors got a shorter-term version of this anyway.)

narrative.text: Senator Mike Crapo introduced the bill on July 28, 2005, with 12 other Republican senators including Senate Majority Leader Bill Frist joining as original cosponsors [S1][S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance [S5].
Seventeen Republican senators signed on as cosponsors [S4].
The Finance Committee never reported the bill, no vote was ever held, and the bill expired when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary taxpayers came out ahead on this bill, since a permanent revenue cut tilted to the wealthiest households never became law. Investors still benefited, because a separate 2006 law extended the same lower rates through 2010.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Taxpayers; investors got a temporary extension anyway

for.name: Mike Crapo
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make the reduced capital gains and dividend rates permanent.

for.name: Bill Frist
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never reported it out, so no vote was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 senators who introduced the bill and all 17 cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored it.

industries.note: Investors who realize capital gains and collect dividends would keep permanently lower tax rates, with the largest gains going to the wealthiest households. The cost is federal revenue that would otherwise be collected mostly from them.

A permanent low rate on gains and dividends makes taxable investment accounts more attractive relative to alternatives, supporting the brokerage and fund industry's business. The benefit is indirect compared to the direct tax savings to investors.
